# CSCI 435 PR review

You are drafting a code review that the user (GitHub login `ab-wm`) will test, edit and post on a
teammate's PR in `CSCI-435-SE/gitea`, a course fork of Gitea. The review is a graded course
deliverable, so the user stays its author: you gather the facts, check them, and hand back a
draft in their format. Don't post, approve or comment on the PR, and don't push to it. Don't offer
to fix the author's code either. In this course the author makes each change themselves, one
change per commit.

The user's standing instruction for reviews is "not *that* deep". That doesn't mean overlooking
real problems, and it doesn't mean nitpicking every small one. The code is not going upstream. A
finding belongs in the draft only if it would change a score, or if the author would want to know
about it before merging.

## 1. Find your footing

Work out where you are running, because that decides how you fetch the PR and where the draft goes.

- **Claude Code inside the repo clone** (`gh` works, and the working tree is the fork). Use `gh`
  for PR data and read source files locally. The user is usually on their own feature branch, so
  don't switch it. Fetch the PR head with `git fetch origin pull/<N>/head:pr-<N>` and read files
  with `git show pr-<N>:<path>`. Compare with `git diff origin/main...pr-<N>`, because local
  `main` is often behind.
- **Chat, or anywhere without the clone.** The repo is public. Use a GitHub connector if one is
  attached. Otherwise fetch the URLs in `references/fetching-without-the-repo.md`. If nothing can
  reach GitHub, ask the user for the PR link and the diff.

## 2. Triage

First get the PR's title, author, changed files and linked issue (`Closes #N`). Then decide how
much review it needs. The user only does a full review when code changed:

- **The PR is already merged, or the user has already reviewed it.** Say so first, quoting their
  existing review in a line. Continue only if they want a fresh look, for example a re-review
  after new commits. Don't let their earlier scores steer yours.
- **The user approved, and commits were pushed after that.** In Sprint 3 a PR may only be merged
  after an approval on its latest commit, so it needs a new approval. Check only the new commits,
  as in a follow-up, and suggest a short re-approval if they're fine.
- **The PR only touches check-ins, docs, course files, showcase material, AI logs, or config like
  `.coderabbit.yaml`.** Skip the rubric. Skim the files for anything surprising, such as code
  hiding in a "docs" PR, a secret, or a file in the wrong folder. Then suggest a one-line
  approval in the user's voice, for example "All good, just the check-in doc and AI log. No need
  for complete review."
- **The PR is a mutation-testing write-up** (`docs/sprint3/mutation/**`). If it holds only the
  write-up and the reports, treat it like a docs PR. If it also adds or changes a test, run that test
  (section 4) and check it the way section 5 describes. Also check that the mutant the write-up says
  it kills shows as killed in the `-after` report. Search the report for that location rather than
  reading it whole, since the reports can be large.
- **The PR is the user's own.** Nobody approves their own PR in this course. Say so, and offer a
  list of findings instead of a rubric.
- **This is a follow-up after the user asked for changes.** Check only the items they asked for.
  If those are done, suggest a short approval such as "All good now!"
- **The PR changes code or tests.** Do the full review described below.

## 3. Gather, lightly

Read these in order, and stop once you can score every rubric row:

1. The PR description, including its `## Test Evidence` section, and the linked issue's
   acceptance criteria (ACs) and design decisions. The rubric is scored against the ACs.
2. The diff. Skip `ai-logs/**`: those files are thousands of lines of chat transcript, and they
   are not reviewed.
3. The review bots' comments and the author's replies, so you don't repeat what was already raised
   and fixed:
   - **CodeRabbit**, configured by the repo's `.coderabbit.yaml`.
   - **Gitar** (Sonar's AI reviewer, mentioned as `@gitar-bot`), if the team turns it on. It keeps
     one dashboard comment that it updates on every push, holding its verdict and, when CI fails, a
     root-cause analysis. It also posts inline findings rated Critical, Important or Minor, and moves
     resolved ones into a collapsed section. Its rules, if any, are in the repo's `.gitar/` folder.
4. The CI status, if you can see it. Gitar's root-cause note on a failure is a lead, not a verdict;
   check it. If the course connects the repo to SonarQube Cloud, its quality gate shows up among the
   PR's checks.
5. SonarQube for IDE, if it's running in the user's VS Code and Claude Code is connected (`/ide`).
   Read its diagnostics for the PR's changed files. Only findings on changed lines count, and each is
   a lead to check like any other finding. If nothing shows, skip this step rather than setting it up.
6. Just enough of the code the diff touches or depends on to check its claims. In the clone,
   `.claude-students/INDEX.md` lists short docs for each area if you need background.

Don't run lint; CI does that. Do run the PR's tests (section 4), so the user doesn't have to. Don't
split the review across subagents.

Aim for about 10–15 tool calls for reading and checking, plus what the test runs need. In testing,
runs that went to 35 calls produced no better drafts than shorter ones would have. Spend those calls
on checking the findings that will go in the draft, one check each. Don't chase ideas you won't
include. Don't read the author's AI logs, and only download a library's source when a finding depends
on it. If you go over the budget, write the draft with what you have, and say what you didn't check.
Reviewers are expected to answer within 24 hours, which is one more reason to keep it short.

## 4. Run the PR's tests

In the clone, run the tests the PR adds or changes, plus the existing test files for the source files
it changes, and record the real counts. In chat you can't run anything: say so, give the user the exact
commands to run, and leave the testing line as a TODO.

- **Work in a throwaway worktree**, so the user's branch and their own server aren't touched:
  `git worktree add --detach .specstory/review-<N> pr-<N>`, then `CI=true pnpm install
  --frozen-lockfile` inside it. Never symlink `node_modules` into a worktree.
- **Unit tests:** `pnpm exec vitest run <files>` for the frontend, and `go test -run '<names>' ./<pkg>/`
  for Go. Go must match `go.mod`: a newer system Go breaks things, so put `~/sdk/go1.26.4/bin` first on
  `PATH` (check `go version` against `go.mod`).
- **Can the new unit tests fail?** This check is cheap. Restore the PR's changed source files to
  `origin/main` in the worktree, re-run the new unit tests, then restore the PR's versions. Tests for
  new behaviour should now fail. One that still passes may not test the change. Use it as evidence for
  the Test coverage row, not as a finding on its own.
- **Playwright tests the PR adds or changes:** `make test-e2e` can't run on this machine.
  1. Build the worktree (`make frontend backend`).
  2. Start its own server from a copy of `custom/conf/app.ini` with `WORK_PATH` set to the worktree
     and port 3001. Start it inside a helper script and stop it by PID, never with `pkill -f`. Create
     the `e2e-admin` user (password `password`) with `./gitea admin user create` if that instance
     doesn't have it.
  3. Run Playwright with a scratch config that extends `playwright.config.ts` and points Chromium at
     `/usr/bin/chromium` (`launchOptions.executablePath`). Set `GITEA_TEST_E2E_URL`,
     `GITEA_TEST_E2E_USER=e2e-admin`, `GITEA_TEST_E2E_PASSWORD=password` and
     `GITEA_TEST_E2E_DOMAIN=localhost`. Run on Chromium and Firefox.

  If the setup still fails after one fix, stop and say so; CI's e2e run is the fallback. The shell is
  zsh, so write environment variables out instead of using unquoted `$VARS`.
- **Read only the summary lines** of each run (pass, fail and skip counts, plus the names of any
  failures), not the full output.
- **A failure isn't a finding yet.** `multiselect-aria.test.ts` already fails locally on untouched
  main, and CI passes it. For any other failure, re-run it on `origin/main`. Only a failure the PR
  causes is a required fix, because the course allows no new test failures.
- **Clean up:** stop the server, then `git worktree remove --force .specstory/review-<N>`.

On a follow-up after new commits, re-run only the tests those commits touch.

## 5. What to check

- **Each AC.** Find where it is implemented and where it is tested. A missing AC is the main
  reason to lower the Correctness score.
- **Whether the tests can fail.** A test that would still pass with the feature removed doesn't
  count as coverage. Look for:
  - assertions that read a value without first asserting it exists;
  - `test.fail()` or skips that cover more than the one known failure;
  - checks that only test whether something is present.
- **The Test Evidence section** (required in every PR since Sprint 3). It needs:
  - one row per AC (for a bug fix, its Expected Behavior; for a PR with no behaviour change, "N/A"
    and a reason);
  - for each row, a named test or "Manual:" steps with what was seen;
  - a Level of unit, integration, E2E or manual;
  - a Source of expected value of AC, issue discussion, docs, upstream behavior, or other
    (explained);
  - a "Not tested automatically, and why" line that lists only the manual ACs;
  - an "AI-written tests" line, saying which tests and how their expected values were checked.

  Spot-check one or two rows: open the test, read its expected value, and compare it with the cited
  source. A value that only matches what the code happens to output (a pasted snapshot, or a number
  the AC never mentions) is exactly what the sprint page rules out.
- **Course rules that graders look at:**
  - `Closes #<N>` in the description, and the PR on the `Sprint 3` milestone;
  - a `## Tech Debt` section;
  - an AI assistance section;
  - before/after screenshots when templates, CSS or Vue files change;
  - Conventional Commit messages that end in `(#N)`;
  - `Assisted-by` trailers, and no `Co-Authored-By`;
  - commits small enough to review, for example split by layer;
  - a skipped test, `test.fail()`, `t.Skip` or disabled CI check has a linked issue and a reason in
    a code comment;
  - no new test failures: a red CI check on code the PR touches is a required fix;
  - commits pushed by a bot (for example a Gitar fix) are AI-made changes, so the AI section should
    mention them.

  A bot's approval (Gitar can auto-approve) doesn't count: the course needs a teammate's approval.

  The current sprint's rules are on https://csci-435-se.github.io/sprint3/. The repo's
  `.claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md` still described Sprint 2 on Nov 4, so where the two
  disagree, the sprint page wins.
- **Claims in the PR description.** Descriptions are often drafted by AI. Check one or two
  concrete claims against the code, such as a timing, a count, or "every test does X".

Check every finding against the source before it goes in the draft. Reviews of AI-written code
tend to produce confident findings that turn out wrong. A wrong finding in a posted review costs
the user more than a missed nit. If checking disproves your idea, drop the finding or reword it.
For example, on #105 a suspected "silent pass" turned out to fail loudly, so the finding became
about the unhelpful error message instead.

Leave out style nits, anything lint or CI catches, CodeRabbit or Gitar findings the author already
fixed (credit those in one line), and anything that wouldn't change a score. A bot or Sonar finding
that's still open goes in the draft only if you checked it against the code yourself. A Sonar rule
that fights Gitea's conventions isn't a finding.

## 6. Scoring

Start every row at 10, and deduct points only for a concrete gap you can name. Past reviews show
how the user scores:

- A UI change without before/after screenshots: Documentation 8, Overall 9, "Yes, once the
  screenshots are added".
- One large commit instead of commits split by layer: AI transparency 7.
- A factual error in the description or the Tech Debt section: Documentation 8.
- Everything checks out: 10s, and Overall 10, "Yes".

A deduction needs a *required* point behind it, something you would ask the author to change before
merging. An observation you'd only file under "Strictly optional" (one AC covered by unit tests but not
end to end, a small AI-assisted commit the description doesn't mention) leaves the score at 10. The user
has scored a feature PR 10 on every row even though optional observations like these existed.

Overall is "Yes" unless something required is missing. Nits don't block a merge. Any score below
7 needs a note saying what would raise it, because the course rubric requires one.

The test-evidence row is new, so there are no posted examples of it yet. Score it like the other
rows. A missing Test Evidence section, an AC with no row, or an expected value with no real source is
a required fix and lowers the score. A source that is valid but could be stronger is optional and
leaves it at 10. The row also asks which tests the reviewer ran locally: answer it from the section 4
runs, with real counts. If nothing could be run, put a visible `TODO (you): which tests you ran
locally` there instead.

## 7. Draft format

Use the rows from the course rubric. Read `.github/code-review-rubric.md` from the repo, or from
raw GitHub, so the draft picks up any change to the rubric. The template below matches the rubric
as of Sprint 3: the sprint page adds the test-evidence row. On Nov 4 the repo's rubric file didn't
have that row yet, so keep it even if the file still lacks it.

Write in the user's voice:

- short, plain sentences;
- one sentence per table note;
- no rule citations in the table;
- `file:line` for code findings.

Skim one of the reviews in `references/posted-examples.md` before you draft. These are reviews
the user actually posted.

```markdown
### Code Review — @ab-wm

Ran the PR's tests locally with Claude Code: <each command or file, with its pass/fail/skip counts>. TODO (you): anything you clicked or checked by hand, or delete this.

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Test evidence — does every AC have a test? Are the expected values justified? Which tests did you run locally? | | <finding>. Ran <which tests> locally: <counts>. |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |

### Strictly optional for completeness
**<the point in a few words>.** <one or two sentences, with file:line>

### AI-Log
Review was drafted by AI, and then changed to better fit the review structure and my inspection of the files. Log available on #<linked issue>.
```

- **Required changes** go in the note of the row they affect, written as a request ("please add
  before/after screenshots, as they are required"). Overall then says "Yes, once X is added".
- **Optional points** go in their own section after the table. Keep at most one or two, and drop
  the section if there are none.
- **The testing line** states only the test runs that really happened in section 4, with their
  counts, and says Claude Code ran them. What the user clicked or checked by hand stays a visible
  `TODO` for them to write or delete. Never fill it with your own checks; a visible placeholder can't
  be posted by accident without being noticed.

## 8. Hand it back

- **In Claude Code**, write the draft to `.specstory/pr-<N>-review.md` (the folder is
  gitignored). If that file already exists, it may be the user's edited copy, so write the draft
  to `pr-<N>-review-2.md` (or the next free number) instead.
- **In chat**, give the draft as one fenced markdown block, so the table copies cleanly.

Then write a short summary in chat, about 10–15 lines:

- the verdict;
- each finding, marked required or optional;
- the test results, and what you didn't run or check (for example, "e2e setup failed, so I relied
  on CI"), so the user knows what is left for them;
- any idea you couldn't verify, offered as something the user could try in their own testing.
  Unverified ideas never go in the draft.

End there. Remind the user to file this session's AI log in `ai-logs/sprint3/ab-wm/`, as
`ai-logs/README.md` describes, since the AI-Log section points to it. If they approve, mention once
that any commit the author pushes afterwards needs a new approval before the merge.

{"author":"CarsonRackley","body":"Closes #118\n\n## What changed\n\n- **Tab icon badge.** `favicon-status.ts` now knows about two badges that can own the tab icon: an Actions run's status and a new unread-notification dot. A single `renderFavicon()` picks one (run status first, then the dot, then the default icon). The dot reuses the run badge's position and white ring, and is filled with `--color-primary` so it matches the navbar's unread bubble. `RepoActionView.vue` is unchanged.\n- **Desktop notification opt-in.** A new **Enable desktop notifications** button on the Notifications page (`notification_div.tmpl`, wired in `features/notification-desktop.ts`). The choice is stored per browser in `localUserSettings`. The browser's permission prompt is only requested from that click, and a denial shows \"Desktop notifications are blocked by your browser.\" Clicking it again disables alerts.\n- **One alert across tabs.** Every Gitea tab already shares one event stream through `eventsource.sharedworker.ts`. Tabs now tell the worker whether they are visible and what their count is. When the count goes up and no Gitea tab is visible, the worker asks exactly one tab (the one used most recently) to show the alert. The decision logic is a small DOM-free class in `modules/notification-alert.ts` so it can be unit tested.\n- **Alert content.** Only a count (\"You have N new notification(s)\", counting since Gitea was last in view); clicking it focuses Gitea and opens `/notifications`. The text reaches every page as `data-` attributes on the navbar count.\n- **Polling fallback.** When the shared worker or event stream is unavailable, a hidden tab that sees the count go up alerts on its own; all alerts share one notification tag so the browser shows one.\n- New locale keys in `locale_en-US.json` only.\n\n## Why\n\nUsers who leave Gitea in a background tab don't notice review requests and mentions until they switch back. {"assignees":["CarsonRackley"],"body":"Part of #7. Upstream requests: go-gitea/gitea#1415 (badge on the favicon) and go-gitea/gitea#31925 (browser notifications).\n\n### User Story\n\nAs a user who keeps Gitea open in a background tab, I want the tab icon to show when I have unread notifications, and optionally a desktop notification when a new one arrives, so that I notice review requests and mentions without switching back to check.\n\n### User Scenario\n\nMarco keeps Gitea open in one of many browser tabs while he codes. On the Notifications page he clicks \"Enable desktop notifications\", and the browser asks for permission once. He allows it. Later a teammate requests his review. A dot appears on the Gitea tab's icon, and a desktop notification says \"You have 1 new notification\". He clicks it, and the browser switches to Gitea and opens his notifications. After he reads it, the unread count drops to zero and the dot disappears. When he is already looking at Gitea, no desktop notification pops up; the navbar count is enough.\n\n### Acceptance Criteria\n\n- [ ] AC1: Given a signed-in user with at least one unread notification, when any Gitea page loads or the unread count updates, then the tab icon shows a badge dot, and when the count drops to 0 the default icon comes back without a reload.\n- [ ] AC2: Given an Actions run page, which already sets the tab icon to the run's status, when the user also has unread notifications, then the run status icon is shown, not the notification badge.\n- [ ] AC3: Given desktop notifications have never been enabled in this browser, when new notifications arrive, then no desktop notification is shown and the browser never asks for permission on its own.\n- [ ] AC4: Given the user clicks \"Enable desktop notifications\" on the Notifications page, when the browser asks for permission and the user denies it, then the page says notifications are blocked by the browser and the setting stays off.\n- [ ] AC5: Given desktop notifications are enabled and permission is granted, when the unread count goes up while the Gitea tab is hidden, then exactly one desktop notification is shown saying how many new notifications there are, without the issue title or repository name.\n- [ ] AC6: Given Gitea is open in several tabs, when the unread count goes up, then the user gets one desktop notification, not one per tab.\n- [ ] AC7: Given the Gitea tab is visible, or the count stays the same or goes down, when the count updates, then no desktop notification is shown.\n- [ ] AC8: Given a desktop notification is shown, when the user clicks it, then the browser focuses Gitea and opens `/notifications`.\n- [ ] AC9: Given desktop notifications are enabled, when the user clicks \"Disable desktop notifications\", then no more desktop notifications are shown in that browser.\n\n### Out of Scope\n\n- Notifications when no Gitea tab is open (Web Push with a service worker and server-side keys).\n- A number inside the badge, or a count in the page title.\n- Per-type or per-repository rules for which notifications alert.\n- Sounds, email, and the mobile or API side of notifications.\n\n### Open Questions\n\n- Should the badge be something the user can turn off? (Proposed: no. It is passive and only appears when there is something unread.)\n- Should the alert also fire when the page falls back to polling because the event stream is unavailable? (Proposed: yes, both update paths behave the same.)\n\n### Design Decisions\n\n#### Decision 1: The desktop notification opt-in is stored per browser, not on the account\n\n**Decision:** \"Enable desktop notifications\" is remembered in the browser's local storage.\n**Alternatives Considered:** (a) A per-user setting stored on the server, shown in Settings. (b) No stored setting: alert whenever the browser permission is granted.\n**Rationale:** Browser permission is per browser and per device anyway, and browsers only allow the permission prompt after a click. A server-side setting would turn on in a browser that never granted permission and would have to prompt without a click, which browsers block. With (b), users who granted permission for something else could not turn the alerts off without revoking it.\n**Consequences:** No server or schema change. The choice does not follow the user to other browsers, and clearing site data turns it off.\n\n#### Decision 2: The desktop notification shows only a count\n\n**Decision:** The notification text is \"You have N new notifications\" and clicking it opens `/notifications`.\n**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Show the newest notification's issue title and repository. (b) Show one notification per new item, each linking to its issue.\n**Rationale:** The live update only delivers a count, so (a) and (b) need an extra API request per update. Titles from private repositories would also appear on a lock screen or a shared screen. A count is enough to make the user switch tabs.\n**Consequences:** The user cannot tell a review request from a subscription update until they open Gitea. Richer content is follow-up work if users ask for it.\n\n#### Decision 3: Badge as a dot, with Actions run status taking precedence\n\n**Decision:** The badge is a plain dot drawn on the Gitea icon, reusing the drawing code that already badges the icon with an Actions run's status. On a run page the run status wins.\n**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Draw the unread number in the icon. (b) Put the count in the page title, like \"(3) Gitea\".\n**Rationale:** A number is unreadable at 16 px and needs a \"9+\" cap. The title is truncated in a crowded tab bar and changes the text screen readers announce. On a run page the user is watching that run, so its status is the more useful icon.\n**Consequences:** The icon code needs to know which badge currently owns the icon, so leaving a run page or reading every notification restores the right one.\n\n### Scope\n\nmedium\n\n---\nDrafted with Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5).\n","milestone":"Sprint 3","title":"Alert me to new notifications with a tab icon badge and opt-in desktop notifications"}

Adding opt-in desktop alerts and cross-tab routing changes notification behavior; the polling fallback can produce duplicate alerts across hidden tabs.

Adds a tab favicon dot for unread notifications and an opt-in, count-only desktop alert that fires once across tabs when Gitea is hidden. Resolved the issue where a throwing `new Notification()` on Android Chrome stopped the poller permanently. No open issues found.

<details>
<summary><kbd>✅ 1 closed</kbd></summary>

<details>
<summary>✅ <b>Bug:</b> new Notification() throwing on Android Chrome stops the poller for good</summary>

> <kbd>📄 web_src/js/features/notification-desktop.ts:10-12</kbd> <kbd>📄 web_src/js/features/notification-desktop.ts:26</kbd> <kbd>📄 web_src/js/features/notification.ts:79</kbd> <kbd>📄 web_src/js/features/notification.ts:85</kbd>
> `notificationApiAvailable()` only checks `'Notification' in window`. Chrome for Android exposes `Notification` and lets you grant permission, but calling `new Notification(...)` there throws `TypeError: Illegal constructor` (it only supports `ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification`). So the toggle shows up, the user enables it, and the first alert throws. On the polling fallback (used where SharedWorker isn't available, which includes mobile browsers), that throw happens at notification.ts:79, before `callback(timeout, newCount)` on line 85 runs. The rejected promise ends the `setTimeout` chain, so the unread count and favicon dot never update again until the page is reloaded. The polling-path alert in notification.ts also has no test. Fix: wrap the constructor in try/catch so a failure can't escape `showDesktopAlert`, and add a test where the stubbed `Notification` constructor throws, checking that polling continues.

</details>

index 0000000000..6abfa386b4
--- /dev/null
+++ b/web_src/js/features/notification-desktop.ts
@@ -0,0 +1,72 @@
+import {localUserSettings} from '../modules/user-settings.ts';
+import {registerGlobalInitFunc} from '../modules/observer.ts';
+import {trN} from '../modules/i18n.ts';
+import {toggleElem} from '../utils/dom.ts';
+
+const {appSubUrl} = window.config;
+// stored per browser, because the permission it depends on is per browser too
+const desktopAlertsSettingKey = 'notification-desktop-alerts';
+
+function notificationApiAvailable(): boolean {
+  return 'Notification' in window;
+}
+
+export function desktopAlertsEnabled(): boolean {
+  // a permission revoked after opting in reads as off
+  return notificationApiAvailable() && Notification.permission === 'granted' && localUserSettings.getBoolean(desktopAlertsSettingKey);
+}
+
+export function showDesktopAlert(newCount: number) {
+  if (newCount <= 0 || !desktopAlertsEnabled()) return;
+  const textEl = document.querySelector('.notification_count')!;
+  // only a count, so no private issue or repo names reach a lock screen
+  const body = trN(newCount, textEl.getAttribute('data-desktop-alert-1')!, textEl.getAttribute('data-desktop-alert-n')!);
+  const icon = document.querySelector<HTMLLinkElement>('link[rel~="icon"]')?.href;
+  // the shared tag makes the browser replace an earlier alert instead of stacking one per update or tab
+  let alert: Notification;
+  try {
+    alert = new Notification(textEl.getAttribute('data-desktop-alert-title')!, {body, icon, tag: `gitea-notifications:${appSubUrl}`});
+  } catch (error) {
+    // e.g. Android Chrome only allows ServiceWorkerRegistration.showNotification; a throw here would stop the count poller
+    console.error(error);
+    return;
+  }
+  alert.addEventListener('click', () => {
+    window.focus();
+    window.location.assign(`${appSubUrl}/notifications`);
+    alert.close();
+  });
+}
+
+export function initNotificationDesktopToggle(el: HTMLElement) {
+  if (!notificationApiAvailable()) return; // the wrapper stays hidden
+  const button = el.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('.notification-desktop-toggle')!;
+  const blocked = el.querySelector('.notification-desktop-blocked')!;
+
+  const render = (showBlocked: boolean) => {
+    const enabled = desktopAlertsEnabled();
+    toggleElem(el.querySelector('.notification-desktop-enable')!, !enabled);
+    toggleElem(el.querySelector('.notification-desktop-disable')!, enabled);
+    toggleElem(blocked, showBlocked);
+    button.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(enabled));
+  };
+
+  button.addEventListener('click', async () => {
+    if (desktopAlertsEnabled()) {
+      localUserSettings.setBoolean(desktopAlertsSettingKey, false);
+      render(false);
+      return;
+    }
+    // browsers only allow the permission prompt from a user click, so this is the one place it is asked
+    const permission = Notification.permission === 'default' ? await Notification.requestPermission() : Notification.permission;
+    localUserSettings.setBoolean(desktopAlertsSettingKey, permission === 'granted');
+    render(permission === 'denied');
+  });
+
+  render(Notification.permission === 'denied');
+  toggleElem(el, true);
+}
+
+export function initNotificationDesktop() {
+  registerGlobalInitFunc('initNotificationDesktopToggle', initNotificationDesktopToggle);
+}

+// Decides, once for all tabs sharing the event stream, whether an unread count change deserves a desktop alert.
+// No DOM access: it runs inside the shared worker.
+
+export type NotificationTabState = {visible: boolean, count: number};
+export type NotificationAlert<Tab> = {tab: Tab, newCount: number};
+
+export class NotificationAlertTracker<Tab> {
+  tabs = new Map<Tab, boolean>(); // tab -> visible
+  lastVisibleTab: Tab | null = null;
+  lastCount: number | null = null;
+  baseline = 0; // the count when the user last had Gitea in view, so "new" means new since then
+
+  anyVisible(): boolean {
+    for (const visible of this.tabs.values()) {
+      if (visible) return true;
+    }
+    return false;
+  }
+
+  setTabState(tab: Tab, {visible, count}: NotificationTabState) {
+    this.tabs.set(tab, visible);
+    if (this.lastCount === null) {
+      this.lastCount = count;
+      this.baseline = count;
+    }
+    if (visible) {
+      this.lastVisibleTab = tab;
+      this.baseline = this.lastCount;
+    }
+  }
+
+  removeTab(tab: Tab) {
+    this.tabs.delete(tab);
+    if (this.lastVisibleTab === tab) this.lastVisibleTab = null;
+  }
+
+  onCount(count: number): NotificationAlert<Tab> | null {
+    const lastCount = this.lastCount;
+    this.lastCount = count;
+    if (this.tabs.size === 0) return null;
+    if (this.anyVisible()) {
+      this.baseline = count;
+      return null;
+    }
+    if (count < this.baseline) this.baseline = count;
+    if (lastCount === null || count <= lastCount) return null;
+    const tab = this.lastVisibleTab ?? this.tabs.keys().next().value!;
+    return {tab, newCount: count - this.baseline};
+  }
+}

function buildStatusIconMarkup(status: ActionsStatus): string {
  const {name, colorClass} = getActionStatusIcon(status, 'circle-fill');
  const color = resolveTailwindTextColor(colorClass);
  const {svgInnerHtml} = svgParseOuterInner(name);
  const coloredInner = svgInnerHtml.replaceAll('currentColor', color);
  const ring = html`<circle cx="${badgeX + badgeCenter}" cy="${badgeY + badgeCenter}" r="${badgeRingRadius}" fill="#ffffff"/>`;
  const badge = html`<g data-actions-status-name="${status}" transform="translate(${badgeX}, ${badgeY}) scale(${badgeScale})" fill="${color}" color="${color}">${htmlRaw(coloredInner)}</g>`;
  return html`${htmlRaw(ring)}${htmlRaw(badge)}`;
}

export function buildStatusFaviconSvg(status: ActionsStatus): string {
  return html`<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="${faviconViewBox}">${htmlRaw(giteaFaviconInner)}${htmlRaw(buildStatusIconMarkup(status))}</svg>`;
}

function buildStatusFaviconDataUrl(status: ActionsStatus): string {
  const cached = faviconDataUrlCache.get(status);
  if (cached) return cached;
  const dataUrl = `data:image/svg+xml,${encodeURIComponent(buildStatusFaviconSvg(status))}`;
  faviconDataUrlCache.set(status, dataUrl);
  return dataUrl;
}

function setFaviconHref(href: string) {
  rememberDefaultFaviconHrefs();
  for (const link of defaultFaviconHrefs.keys()) {
    if (link.isConnected) link.href = href;
  }
}

const {appSubUrl, sharedWorkerUri} = window.config;

export class UserEventsSharedWorker {
  sharedWorker: SharedWorker;

  // options can be either a string (the debug name of the worker) or an object of type WorkerOptions
  constructor(options?: string | WorkerOptions) {
    const worker = new SharedWorker(sharedWorkerUri, options);
    this.sharedWorker = worker;
    worker.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
      console.error('worker error', event);
    });
    worker.port.addEventListener('messageerror', () => {
      console.error('unable to deserialize message');
    });
    worker.port.postMessage({
      type: 'start',
      url: `${window.location.origin}${appSubUrl}/user/events`,
    });
    worker.port.addEventListener('error', (e) => {
      console.error('worker port error', e);
    });
    window.addEventListener('beforeunload', () => {
      // FIXME: this logic is not quite right.
      // "beforeunload" can be canceled by some actions like "are-you-sure" and the navigation can be cancelled.
      // In this case: the worker port is incorrectly closed while the page is still there.
      worker.port.postMessage({type: 'close'});
      worker.port.close();
    });
  }

  addMessageEventListener(listener: (event: MessageEvent) => void) {
    this.sharedWorker.port.addEventListener('message', (event: MessageEvent) => {
      if (!event.data || !event.data.type) {
        console.error('unknown worker message event', event);
        return;
      }

      if (event.data.type === 'error') {
        console.error('worker port event error', event.data);
      } else if (event.data.type === 'logout') {
        if (event.data.data !== 'here') return;
        this.sharedWorker.port.postMessage({type: 'close'});
        this.sharedWorker.port.close();
        // slightly delay our "logout" for a short while, in case there are other logout requests in-flight.
        // * if the logout is triggered by a page redirection (e.g.: user clicks "/user/logout")
        //   * "beforeunload" event is triggered, this code path won't execute
        // * if the logout is triggered by a fetch call
        //   * "beforeunload" event is not triggered until JS does the redirection.
        //     * in this case, the logout fetch call already completes and has sent the "logout" message to the worker
        //   * there can be a data-race between the fetch call's redirection and the "logout" message from the worker
        //     * the fetch call's logout redirection should always win over the worker message, because it might have a custom location
        setTimeout(() => { window.location.assign(`${appSubUrl}/`) }, 1000);
      } else if (event.data.type === 'close') {
        this.sharedWorker.port.postMessage({type: 'close'});
        this.sharedWorker.port.close();
      }
      listener(event);
    });
  }

  postMessage(message: {type: string, [key: string]: any}) {
    this.sharedWorker.port.postMessage(message);
  }

  startPort() {
    this.sharedWorker.port.start();
  }
}

// the navbar count every signed-in page renders, and the toggle notification_div.tmpl renders
function setupPage() {
  document.body.innerHTML = `
    <span class="notification_count" data-desktop-alert-title="Gitea" data-desktop-alert-1="You have %d new notification" data-desktop-alert-n="You have %d new notifications">0</span>`;
  const toggle = createElementFromHTML<HTMLElement>(`
    <div class="tw-hidden">
      <button type="button" class="notification-desktop-toggle">
        <span class="notification-desktop-enable">Enable desktop notifications</span>
        <span class="notification-desktop-disable tw-hidden">Disable desktop notifications</span>
      </button>
      <span class="notification-desktop-blocked tw-hidden">Desktop notifications are blocked by your browser.</span>
    </div>`);
  document.body.append(toggle);
  initNotificationDesktopToggle(toggle);
  const visible = (selector: string) => !toggle.querySelector(selector)!.classList.contains('tw-hidden');
  const button = toggle.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>('.notification-desktop-toggle')!;
  return {toggle, button, visible};
}

// these tests share document.body and the stubbed globals, so they must not run concurrently
describe('desktop notifications', {concurrent: false}, () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    document.documentElement.lang = 'en-US'; // trN resolves plural rules from the document language
    vi.stubGlobal('localStorage', new Storage()); // Node's own localStorage global hides happy-dom's
    FakeNotification.permission = 'default';
    FakeNotification.requestPermission = vi.fn();
    FakeNotification.shown = [];
    vi.stubGlobal('Notification', FakeNotification);
  });
  afterEach(() => {
    vi.restoreAllMocks();
    vi.unstubAllGlobals();
    document.body.replaceChildren();
  });

  test('AC3 never enabled: no alert and no permission prompt', () => {
    const {toggle, visible} = setupPage();
    showDesktopAlert(1);
    expect(FakeNotification.shown).toHaveLength(0);
    expect(FakeNotification.requestPermission).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
    expect(toggle.classList.contains('tw-hidden')).toBe(false);
    expect(visible('.notification-desktop-enable')).toBe(true);
  });

  test('AC3 permission granted for something else does not turn alerts on by itself', () => {
    FakeNotification.permission = 'granted';
    setupPage();
    showDesktopAlert(1);
    expect(FakeNotification.shown).toHaveLength(0);
  });

  test('AC4 denying the browser prompt says it is blocked and leaves the setting off', async () => {
    FakeNotification.requestPermission.mockResolvedValue('denied');
    const {button, visible} = setupPage();
    button.click();
    await vi.waitFor(() => expect(visible('.notification-desktop-blocked')).toBe(true));
    expect(FakeNotification.requestPermission).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);
    expect(desktopAlertsEnabled()).toBe(false);
    expect(visible('.notification-desktop-enable')).toBe(true);
  });

  test('allowing the browser prompt turns alerts on', async () => {
    FakeNotification.requestPermission.mockImplementation(() => {
      FakeNotification.permission = 'granted';
      return Promise.resolve('granted');
    });
    const {button, visible} = setupPage();
    button.click();
    await vi.waitFor(() => expect(visible('.notification-desktop-disable')).toBe(true));
    expect(desktopAlertsEnabled()).toBe(true);
    expect(visible('.notification-desktop-blocked')).toBe(false);
  });

  test('AC5 the alert says how many new notifications there are and nothing else', () => {
    FakeNotification.permission = 'granted';
    const {button} = setupPage();
    button.click(); // permission is already granted, so this enables without a prompt
    showDesktopAlert(1);
    showDesktopAlert(3);
    expect(FakeNotification.requestPermission).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
    expect(FakeNotification.shown.map((n) => n.options.body)).toEqual(['You have 1 new notification', 'You have 3 new notifications']);
    expect(FakeNotification.shown[0].title).toBe('Gitea');
  });

  test('AC8 clicking the alert focuses Gitea and opens the notifications page', () => {
    FakeNotification.permission = 'granted';
    const {button} = setupPage();
    button.click();
    const focus = vi.spyOn(window, 'focus').mockImplementation(() => {});
    const assign = vi.spyOn(window.location, 'assign').mockImplementation(() => undefined);
    showDesktopAlert(1);
    FakeNotification.shown[0].dispatchEvent(new Event('click'));
    expect(focus).toHaveBeenCalled();
    expect(assign).toHaveBeenCalledWith('/notifications');
    expect(FakeNotification.shown[0].close).toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  test('a browser that refuses to construct the alert does not make showDesktopAlert throw', () => {
    FakeNotification.permission = 'granted';
    const {button} = setupPage();
    button.click();
    // Android Chrome exposes Notification but its constructor throws "Illegal constructor"
    class ThrowingNotification extends FakeNotification {
      constructor(title: string, options: NotificationOptions) {
        super(title, options);
        throw new TypeError('Illegal constructor');
      }
    }
    vi.stubGlobal('Notification', ThrowingNotification);
    const consoleError = vi.spyOn(console, 'error').mockImplementation(() => {});
    expect(() => showDesktopAlert(1)).not.toThrow();
    expect(consoleError).toHaveBeenCalled();
  });

  test('AC9 disabling stops further alerts', async () => {
    FakeNotification.permission = 'granted';
    const {button, visible} = setupPage();
    button.click();
    expect(visible('.notification-desktop-disable')).toBe(true);
    button.click();
    await vi.waitFor(() => expect(visible('.notification-desktop-enable')).toBe(true));
    showDesktopAlert(1);
    expect(FakeNotification.shown).toHaveLength(0);
  });
});
